analysis.one_liner: Bans race-based preferences in federal contracting, employment, and federally funded programs.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to four House committees on the day it was introduced and never received a committee vote or floor action before the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would bar the federal government and any entity receiving federal money from discriminating against or giving preference to anyone based on race, color, or national origin in contracts, employment, or school admissions. It defines preference broadly to include quotas, set-asides, and numerical goals, and it lets individuals sue violators with attorney's fees awarded if they win. It was referred to four House committees on March 9, 2023 and never moved from there.
analysis.who_benefits: People who believe they were passed over for a federal job, contract, or school admission because of their race or national origin would get a new right to sue, with attorney's fees paid if they win. Federal agencies and contractors would no longer run race-conscious set-aside or quota programs.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People who say they were passed over due to race preferences

how_it_helps.text: Creates a private right of action: anyone harmed by a race-based preference or discrimination in a federal program can sue, including against government entities, and recovers attorney's fees and possibly back pay [S3].
Requires every federal agency to review and modify its policies within six months to remove race, color, or national origin preferences [S3].
Defines preference to cover quotas, set-asides, numerical goals, and timetables, so race-conscious targets in contracting and employment would be prohibited outright [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Federal agencies, federal contractors, and colleges would have to dismantle race-conscious programs. Minority-owned and other businesses that currently benefit from federal set-aside programs would lose that channel of federal work, and entities could face lawsuits under the new private right of action.
analysis.who_pays_short: Agencies, contractors, universities, and set-aside beneficiaries

drawbacks.text: It would end not only quotas but narrowly tailored race-conscious programs, such as minority business set-asides, that Congress and agencies created to counter documented discrimination in federal contracting [S2].

The private right of action with mandatory attorney's fees could generate substantial litigation against universities, school districts, and agencies over any policy that considers race, color, or national origin [S3].
An honest supporter would acknowledge that race-neutral rules alone leave no tool for remedying discrimination that has already occurred in federal contracting and employment.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The tradeoff is genuinely contested. Supporters see the bill as enforcing equal treatment: no one loses a federal job, contract, or admission because of race. Critics see it as dismantling remedies for discrimination while the private right of action turns any race-conscious policy into a lawsuit. Because it defines preference to include even flexible numerical goals, the bill reaches further than current law requires, and the costs would fall on the same programs designed to widen access to federal work. The bill never advanced far enough for Congress to weigh these tradeoffs in a hearing or vote.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to four House committees the day it was introduced, none of them ever acted on it, and the bill died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Thomas Tiffany introduced the bill on March 9, 2023 [S1].
It was referred the same day to the House Judiciary, Oversight and Accountability, Education and the Workforce, and House Administration committees [S5].
Eleven Republicans cosponsored the bill; no Democrat did [S4].
The action history shows no committee vote, hearing, or floor action after the referral [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nothing changed. Federal agencies, contractors, and universities kept operating under existing law, so businesses and institutions running race-conscious programs, and the people who benefit from them, are better off than they would have been under the bill. The bill's supporters did not get a vote on it either.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Beneficiaries of existing race-conscious programs kept status quo

for.name: Reps. Burgess Owens, Michelle Steel, and Byron Donalds

against.name: House Judiciary Committee (Chair Jim Jordan, R-OH)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a markup or vote after its referral

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 11 cosponsors were House Republicans; no Democrat signed on, and with no roll call taken, the record shows only a one-sided roster of support.

industries.industry: Businesses in federal minority and disadvantaged business set-aside programs
industries.note: The bill's broad definition of preference would prohibit the race-based set-asides and numerical goals these programs rely on, ending a channel of guaranteed federal work. Supporters argue equal treatment; opponents argue the programs exist to counter measured discrimination in contracting.

As recipients of federal financial assistance, they could no longer consider race in admissions or run race-conscious hiring, and could be sued for doing so. Supporters call this equal protection; critics call it removing tools for campus diversity.

They lose any race-conscious program obligations but also gain protection from the government pressuring them into preferences, and individuals gain a new way to sue them. The net effect cuts in both directions.
